extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, publishers, and biomedical researchers (authors and readers interested in research integrity and retraction practices)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards for when and how scientific articles should be retracted, how journals and institutions should respond to suspected misconduct or error, and how to measure retraction frequency. Intended to inform editorial policy and research-community practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasons for retraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles may be retracted when their findings are no longer considered trustworthy due to scientific misconduct or error, they plagiarize previously published work, or they are found to violate ethical guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from Infection and Immunity include inappropriate digital-figure manipulation, inability to confirm original results, miscoded/incorrect biological materials, impure critical reagents, and extensive plagiarism. A COPE survey (Medline retractions 1988–2004) found ~40% due to honest error/nonreplicable findings, 28% research misconduct, 17% redundant publication, and 15% other or unstated reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research misconduct definitions (falsification and fabrication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Research misconduct is classified as falsification or fabrication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Falsification = manipulation of materials, processes, or data to misrepresent results. Fabrication = reporting results of experiments that were not actually performed. These definitions follow standard regulatory usage (e.g., COPE, NSF).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism and self-plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Plagiarism refers to the misrepresentation of another's ideas or words as one's own and includes self-plagiarism (redundant publication or recycling large sections of text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ASM journals strictly prohibit plagiarism and self-plagiarism. While some debate cultural relativity of plagiarism, the authors reject that view and emphasize original wording; detection technologies exist to help identify plagiarism or redundant publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction reserved for major errors or misconduct; errata for minor errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Retractions are reserved for major errors or misconduct that call the conclusions of an article into question; errata or authors' corrections are used to rectify minor errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction is codified in ASM instructions to authors. Journals should apply retraction only when conclusions are undermined, using errata for corrections that do not invalidate the main findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image processing and digital-image-manipulation policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Image processing is acceptable only if applied to all parts of an image; inappropriate digital-image manipulation is a ground for retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should address manipulation explicitly (as ASM does). Editors are referred to extended commentaries (e.g., Journal of Cell Biology) for examples of inappropriate manipulation and for guidance on acceptable processing. Repeated instances of manipulated figures have led to multiple retractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary responsibility for investigating misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary responsibility for investigating possible scientific misconduct rests with the author's institution (and with the Office of Research Integrity when U.S. DHHS funding is involved), not primarily with journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If editors suspect problems, they may request raw data from authors; if misconduct is suspected they should contact the institution and recommend an inquiry. After an institution determines misconduct occurred, journals are obligated to consider retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor actions when suspecting invalid data
rubrics_metrics.description: If an editor has concerns about the validity of data in a submitted or published manuscript, the editor may request that authors provide their raw data for review and may contact the author's institution if misconduct is suspected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should perform independent review of evidence, request author responses, consult with multiple editors and governing editorial boards, and follow institutional findings when deciding on retraction. Without access to raw data, reviewers/editors cannot be expected to detect all falsification/fabrication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may initiate a retraction and how to mark retracted articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Either publishers or authors may initiate a retraction; retraction notices are posted in PubMed and pdf versions of retracted articles should carry a watermark informing readers that the article has been retracted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors are consulted regarding wording, but final wording and decisions are at the journal's discretion. Marking (e.g., PubMed posting and watermarking PDFs) helps inform readers that the record has been corrected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction notice content and transparency (COPE guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Retraction notices should state who is issuing the retraction and the reason for the retraction in order to distinguish misconduct from error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The goal is to be clear, accurate, and fair to both authors and readers. Transparency is recommended (advocated by Retraction Watch and COPE). Giving authors excessive latitude in wording is probably inadvisable; notices should provide sufficient information about the issuer and cause while balancing privacy/fairness concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction index (metric for frequency of retraction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Retraction index = (number of retractions in a given interval) × 1,000 ÷ (number of published articles with abstracts) — used here for the interval 2001–2010.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The retraction index is a simple per-journal metric for frequency of retracted articles. In the authors' analysis it showed a strong correlation with journal impact factor (Spearman P < 0.0001), but the metric should be interpreted cautiously and in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive caution about correlation with impact factor
rubrics_metrics.description: A correlation between a journal's retraction index and its impact factor does not imply causality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple possible explanations exist: (a) higher reward/incentive for groundbreaking papers in high-impact journals could encourage risk-taking or fraud; (b) editorial preference for clear definitive reports might tempt authors to manipulate data; (c) higher-visibility journals attract greater scrutiny leading to more detections. The finding argues for caution in using simple bibliometric measures (e.g., impact factor) as proxies for research quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Republication after retraction — conditional possibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A retracted article may, in theory, be revised and republished after removal of erroneous, falsified, fabricated, or plagiarized content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice, republication can be difficult: journals may impose sanctions prohibiting resubmission for a period, stigma and loss of trust complicate later submissions, and the passage of time may reduce significance. Nevertheless, documented instances exist in which corrected work was republished.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of retraction and persistence of erroneous citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Retractions often do not occur for years after publication, and retracted articles can continue to be cited for long periods after retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because detection and institutional investigations can be slow, erroneous information can remain in circulation. This underscores the importance of vigilance, robust detection tools, prompt institutional inquiry, and clear retraction notices to reduce ongoing miscitation and harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of detection technologies and limits of ethics instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Technology can facilitate detection of plagiarism and redundant publication; formal ethics instruction for trainees has been increased but evidence for effectiveness is limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals and institutions should use available technological tools to detect plagiarism/redundancy. However, educational approaches alone may not sufficiently prevent misconduct given strong external incentives; systemic incentive structures should be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: ASM-specific instructions and enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: ASM journals have specific guidelines in the Instructions to Authors that define plagiarism, fabrication, manipulation or falsification of data, and distinguish retractions from errata.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ASM addresses manipulation of computer-generated images (acceptable only if applied to all parts of an image) and strictly prohibits plagiarism and self-plagiarism. Editors may consult these instructions and ASM Publications Board when handling retraction decisions.
